transcript: There comes a moment in every person's life where the certainty of childhood gives way to questions where you have to decide what beliefs are yours and what beliefs you've inherited. And that is at the forefront of The Saviors, a new play currently running at Atlantic Theater Company. It's about two altar boys whose lives revolve around each other and the church. They're best friends who have always imagined growing up together, going to the same college, having the same future. But the arrival of a stranger at their church cracks open everything they thought they knew. And suddenly faith, friendship and identity all seems uncertain. I have a lot of complicated feelings around religion. I really wasn't sure how I was going to feel about this play, but well I'll let you go is one of my favorite plays of the year. And Bubba Weiler who wrote this, wrote the saviors and Jack Serio who directed this, directed the saviors. So I was intrigued and I'm so glad I did cause I was just so grabbed by this play. It's really because of these two boys, Julius Rinzel and Ivan Howe They are 14 years old and they are absolutely astonishing as Michael and Paul. They're so funny and awkward and vulnerable and brave and you just feel their youth and their confusion and their joy. And they're caring for each other in every single moment. because Paul and Michael care about each other so much in slightly Different ways. And yet they're being pulled apart by their belief and their faith and the world. Michael doesn't want to examine his feelings. He wants to throw himself into his future and his faith. He spends a lot of time talking about the saint he's going to pick for his confirmation name And the rituals and the certainty of the church are easier for him to understand than his own feelings. While Paul sees Michael very clearly and knows that the church is not a safe place for him. And in that discovery, is starting to question everything he knows about the church, his faith, and the life that hasn't mapped out for him. He just doesn't know if it feels right anymore. They are both desperately clinging to each other. As they pull apart from each other. They're also trying to save the other one, when really they should be trying to save themselves. Going with the choice to cast actual young teens in these roles was so important because I just don't think the show works without it. And Jack and Bubba have created, like, such a sense of grounded reality. Feel like I was watching a play. It kind of felt like I was almost eavesdropping into a conversation. It is a deeply beautiful and honest and painful coming of age friendship play, and you should go see it because I haven't stopped thinking about it. It's playing until August 15th at the Linda Gross Theatre.
